title: Fridge Hack Hits Hundreds of French Supermarkets as Nvidia's China AI Chip Share Slips to 34%
subhead: A cyberattack forced refrigeration systems in several hundred French stores up to 50C, causing fires and food losses, while an IDC report shows Nvidia's share of China's data-centre AI chip market fell to 34% as Huawei closed the gap.

sections.heading: Cyberattack Turns French Supermarket Fridges into Heaters
sections.body:
Hackers raised the temperature of connected refrigeration systems in several hundred French supermarkets overnight into Oct 12, pushing fridges to 50C for six hours and triggering fires and food losses, according to the Guardian. The Paris prosecutor's office confirmed a large-scale attack on 'connected refrigerators in several major food retailers across France.'

Les Mousquetaires, owner of Intermarché, said about 150 of its stores were hit and that it discarded all food to avoid health risks. Coopérative U chief executive Dominique Schelcher called the targeting of equipment 'essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people' a matter of 'extreme gravity,' writing on X. BFM TV reported that E Leclerc, France's largest chain, was also affected. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu directed the national cybersecurity agency ANSSI to investigate, and officials said France was coordinating with European counterparts because other countries may be affected.

A source close to Lecornu told the Guardian that ANSSI identified a vulnerability in refrigeration software supplied by Danish firm Danfoss. Danfoss confirmed 'incidents in France affecting a limited number of refrigeration management systems' and said the affected units 'were running outdated firmware.' Separately, Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize reported a 'security issue' in its network affecting Albert Heijn systems, though the Guardian noted it was not clear whether the two events were linked.

This is a rare case of a cyber intrusion producing immediate physical-world damage — not data theft but spoiled food and fires — against civilian retail infrastructure rather than a military or government target.
sections.whyItMatters: It shows that insecure industrial IoT (firmware, not nation-state-grade weapons) can cause tangible physical disruption at scale, and that European food logistics is an exposed target. Macron had already ordered critical-infrastructure protections against what Paris calls Russian 'hybrid attacks.'

sections.heading: Nvidia's China AI Chip Share Falls to 34% as Huawei Closes the Gap
sections.body:
Nvidia's share of China's data-centre AI chip market fell to 34% in the first half of 2026, according to an IDC report seen by Reuters, as US export controls restricted supplies of its products and domestic rivals led by Huawei gained ground. The figure marks a sharp decline from Nvidia's historical dominance of the segment before controls tightened.

The finding underscores a pattern now visible across the market: export restrictions have constrained Nvidia's China revenue while accelerating demand for domestic substitutes. The Reuters report attributes the shift directly to supply restrictions rather than a drop in Chinese appetite for AI compute.

The same day, the Global Times reported that South Korean conglomerate SK Group plans to open an AI R&D centre in Shanghai, covering AI data centres, physical AI and biopharmaceuticals. At the Shanghai International Business Leaders Advisory Council, SK chairman Chey Tae-won said SK had invested around $60 billion in China across semiconductors, batteries and petrochemicals, calling it 'the largest foreign investor in China over the past 35 years.' Chey warned that 'it doesn't seem very wise to think that we can stop China's semiconductor industry,' citing the pace of CXMT and YMTC, and saying of Chinese rivals, 'if you leave them alone, they'll catch up in every area.'

Korea Customs data released the same day showed South Korea's exports to China soared 167% to $7.59 billion in the first ten days of October, driven by the memory upcycle.
sections.whyItMatters: The 34% figure is the clearest gauge yet that controls are reshaping market share rather than eliminating China's AI compute base — they are handing share to Huawei and its domestic peers. SK's Shanghai R&D move, meanwhile, shows a Korean chip giant betting on Chinese market access even as Washington pushes for decoupling.

sections.heading: Super Micro Contractor Pleads Guilty in $2.5B AI Server Smuggling Case
sections.body:
Ting-Wei 'Willy' Sun, a contractor linked to Super Micro Computer, pleaded guilty in US District Court in Manhattan on four counts tied to an illegal scheme to ship Nvidia-powered AI servers to China, according to Reuters. The charges cover conspiracies to breach US export controls, unlawfully remove goods from the country, defraud the government, and obstruct justice; sentencing is set for September 2027.

Prosecutors charged Sun and two others in March with diverting roughly $2.5 billion worth of US AI technology to China starting around October 2023, shipping servers through a Southeast Asian intermediary. Court documents describe Sun as a broker and 'fixer' who arranged transactions and, per the indictment, placed fake 'dummy' servers on-site in December 2025 and lied to a US Commerce Department official inspecting units that had already been exported. The indictment names Nvidia's B200, H100 and H200 GPUs as subject to restrictions.

Two co-defendants were also named: Super Micro co-founder Yih-Shyan 'Wally' Liaw, who has pleaded not guilty and left the board, and Taiwan-based sales manager Ruei-Tsang 'Steven' Chang, who has not appeared in court. Super Micro is not a defendant and said the case has no impact on its operations.
sections.whyItMatters: It is a concrete test of how leaky the enforcement perimeter remains: billions in restricted AI hardware moved through intermediaries before anyone was caught. The conviction signals that the US is pursuing individual brokers and executives, not just companies, in export-control cases.

sections.heading: Samsung Posts Record ~$80B Profit, but AI Chip Stocks Sell Off
sections.body:
Samsung Electronics estimated third-quarter operating profit at 107.4 trillion won (about $80.2 billion), a first for any technology company, on booming AI memory demand, according to Reuters. The figure reflects a roughly nine-fold jump in earnings year-on-year.

Yet the market reaction was negative. According to a market report compiled by the VEST newsletter (citing Korean exchange data), South Korea's KOSPI fell 3.65% to 6,384.24 on Oct 13, with Samsung sold off despite the record result as a broader memory-chip sell-off spread to US markets (Nasdaq down 0.44%) and Nikkei futures fell 1,090 yen. Analysts, per Reuters, had already trimmed Samsung profit forecasts by nearly 8% since late August, and flagged that chip margins may stay flat.

Separately, Reuters reported that TSMC is expected to post a sixth consecutive quarter of record profit, driven by AI infrastructure spending.
sections.whyItMatters: The gap between record profits and a sharp sell-off shows investors are pricing in peak-cycle risk — the memory boom may be nearing its margin limits even as revenue climbs. It is a reminder that headline AI-chip demand and stock-market conviction are no longer moving together.

sections.heading: EnergyX Signs $2B Lithium Deal; US Pushes Deeper into African Minerals
sections.body:
Lithium startup EnergyX said on Oct 12 it signed a $2 billion binding offtake to supply commodities trader Trafigura with battery-grade lithium from Chile and the US, according to Reuters — described as one of the largest deals ever tied to direct lithium extraction technology. The 10-year agreement would move DLE from pilot scale toward commercial volumes.

On the mining-access front, the Trump administration is looking to increase funding for African mining projects as Washington seeks to reduce reliance on Chinese mineral processing, according to reporting summarized by MSN. Semafor reported a battlefield clash in DR Congo involving a US private security contractor, against the backdrop of Washington seeking greater access to Congolese minerals.

Elsewhere, India is planning a strategic reserve of critical minerals to shield its EV, battery, defence and clean-energy industries from supply shocks, per Firstpost.
sections.whyItMatters: Western and Indian governments are converging on the same playbook — locking up upstream supply and stockpiling — while a private-sector DLE deal shows the technology is finally attracting trader-scale offtake. The competition is shifting from refining dominance to who controls the raw ore and the financing behind it.

sections.heading: SpaceX and Amazon Advance Competing Satellite Broadband Empires
sections.body:
SpaceX launched 21 military-network satellites from Vandenberg and was preparing to send up 27 more Starlink craft, according to MSN, part of a tightly packed launch sequence. Reuters reported last week that SpaceX struck a deal to acquire a nationwide low-band spectrum portfolio, moving Musk's venture closer to challenging US wireless carriers directly with orbital mobile service.

Amazon has manufactured its 1,000th satellite for its Leo broadband constellation and is preparing to launch commercial internet service this year, per Cord Cutters News. AST SpaceMobile saw its next BlueBird satellites arrive at Cape Canaveral, per 247wallst. And Banglalink, a VEON subsidiary, announced a partnership with SpaceX to launch South Asia's first direct-to-device Starlink mobile service in Bangladesh, according to SatNews.
sections.whyItMatters: Direct-to-device and low-band spectrum moves blur the line between satellite operators and terrestrial carriers, putting constellations into direct competition with established telecoms. Amazon reaching 1,000 satellites marks the point where a genuine second global constellation is becoming operational rather than aspirational.

bottomLine: Today's developments point in one direction: controls and competition are rearranging who supplies critical technology, not removing anyone from the field. Nvidia's China AI-chip share fell to 34% as Huawei filled the gap, and a Super Micro-linked contractor admitted to smuggling $2.5 billion in restricted servers — evidence that export enforcement is porous even as it intensifies. In France, a firmware vulnerability in industrial refrigeration software let attackers turn supermarket fridges into 50C heaters, a rare case of cyber intrusion causing physical damage to civilian infrastructure. Meanwhile Samsung's record $80 billion profit met a 3.65% KOSPI sell-off, a sign investors see the memory boom cresting. Watch three things next: whether ANSSI's Danfoss finding forces mandatory firmware rules in Europe, whether Nvidia's China share keeps sliding, and whether SpaceX's spectrum move triggers a regulatory fight with US carriers.
sources: Reuters, The Guardian, CBS News, Seattle Times, The Telegraph, Global Times, Korea Customs Service via Yonhap, VEST market report, Firstpost, EnergyX via Reuters, Semafor, Cord Cutters News, 247wallst, SatNews, MSN
